text: Question two. What is the KV cache, and how large does it get? During decode, each new token attends to every token before it. Recomputing their keys and values at every step would be quadratic waste, so they're cached. Per sequence, its size is two, for one key and one value, times the layers, the KV heads, the head dimension, the tokens, and the bytes per value. This model has eighty layers and eight KV heads of dimension a hundred and twenty-eight, at sixteen bits. That's three hundred and twenty kibibytes for every token. One context of a hundred and twenty-eight K tokens takes forty gibibytes, beside about a hundred and forty gigabytes of weights. Now the last step, the one to do on the whiteboard: how many requests fit? Eight eighty-gigabyte GPUs, minus the weights, leave five hundred gigabytes. At eight K tokens a request, at most a hundred and eighty-six fit. At a hundred and twenty-eight K, eleven. Memory, not compute, usually caps how many requests a GPU serves at once, and this cache is where the memory goes. That's why grouped-query attention matters: several query heads share one key and value head. Give each of the sixty-four query heads its own, and the cache grows eight times: twenty-three of those eight K requests, not a hundred and eighty-six. So memory caps the batch, and the next question is how to keep it full.
